steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our VoxGenesis paper on unsupervised discovery of a latent speaker manifold for speech synthesis. Explain why current speech synthesis can't generate new voices, why a speaker latent space would be useful and hard to learn, the limits of the closest prior method, how VoxGenesis works at a high level, and our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Deep generative models and the limits of speech synthesis
2. Benefits of a speaker latent space and why it is hard to learn
3. Prior speaker generation (TacoSpawn) and its limitations
4. VoxGenesis overview
5. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Generative models and speech synthesis
- breakthroughs: GPT, GAN, VAE, more recently DDPM
- realistic images, conversations with humans, intricate programs
- speech synthesis: virtually indistinguishable from human speech
- but success confined to replicating voices of training/reference speakers; unlike image synthesis (unseen scenes, faces), most models can't generate new, unheard voices
- cause: speaker encoders and neural vocoders are deterministic modules mapping speaker embeddings to target waveforms

2. Speaker latent space
- generative models: control over generation, latent space manipulation to edit aspects without attribute labels
- important for speech: emotion, intonation, speaker styles hard to label
- speaker latent space -> sophisticated voice editing, customization, more applications
- hard: speaker characteristics entangled with semantic content; can't directly fit distribution over speech and keep control of content
- disentangling content from speaker features is necessary first step

3. TacoSpawn
- fits GMM over Tacotron2 speaker embeddings, prior over speakers
- can generate novel speakers but: (1) separate parameterization of speaker embedding table and speaker generation model; (2) mixture trained on likelihood of speaker embeddings not data likelihood -> limited representational capability

4. VoxGenesis
- unsupervised generative model, distribution over voice manifold
- transforms Gaussian into speech distribution conditioned on semantic tokens
- vs GAN vocoders (Mel-GAN, HIFI-GAN, SpeechResynthesis): deterministic mapping features -> waveforms
- Figure 1: VoxGenesis vs SpeechResynthesis
- mapping network: isotropic -> non-isotropic Gaussian, control module (yellow box) finds major variances
- shared embedding layer for discriminator; semantic transformation matrices
- vs Style-GAN, BigGAN: Gaussian constrained encoder -> stabilizes training, encodes external speaker representations

5. Contributions
- general framework for unsupervised voice generation (Gaussian -> speech distribution)
- unsupervised editing of gender characteristics, pitch, tone, emotions
- implicit sampling process with speaker embeddings for GANs; divergence term constraining embedding distributions; conventional speaker encoder as part of generative model; encode and modify external speakers

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Deep generative models have changed many fields, with several breakthroughs such as the Generative Pretrained Transformer (GPT), the Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), the Variational Autoencoder (VAE), and more recently Denoising Diffusion Models (DDPM). These models can generate realistic images, take part in conversations with humans and write intricate programs. When they are used for speech synthesis, they can produce speech that is virtually indistinguishable from human speech. But this success is mostly limited to copying the voices of the training or reference speakers. Unlike image synthesis, where models can produce realistic scenes and faces that were never seen, most speech synthesis models cannot generate new voices that were never heard. We argue that this limitation mostly comes from how the speaker encoders and neural vocoders are designed. Usually they work as deterministic modules that map speaker embeddings to the target waveforms.

Apart from the obvious advantage of being able to generate new objects, generative models also allow control over the generation process and allow manipulating the latent space to edit specific aspects of the generated objects without needing attribute labels. This is especially important for speech, because nuanced characteristics like emotion, intonation and speaker styles are hard to label. Having a speaker latent space could make more sophisticated voice editing and customization possible, which would expand the possible applications of speech synthesis a lot. But learning the speaker distribution is not easy. The reason is the intrinsic complexity of speech signals, where the characteristics specific to the speaker are entangled with the semantic content information. So we cannot just fit a distribution over speech directly and expect the model to generate new speakers while still keeping control over the content information. Disentangling content from speaker features is a necessary first step. In prior work, the authors proposed TacoSpawn, a method that fits a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) over Tacotron2 speaker embeddings to learn a prior distribution over speakers. TacoSpawn does offer the capability to generate novel speakers, but it has its own limitations. First, the speaker embedding table and the speaker generation model are parameterized separately, which keeps the synthesis modules from fully benefiting from the generative approach. Second, unlike modern deep generative models, the mixture model in TacoSpawn is trained to maximize the likelihood of the speaker embeddings and not the data likelihood, which limits the representational capability of the generative model.

[VoxGenesis]
- unsupervised generative model, distribution over the voice manifold
- Gaussian -> speech distribution conditioned on semantic tokens
- contrast: GAN vocoders Mel-GAN, HIFI-GAN, SpeechResynthesis = deterministic mapping
- Figure 1 vs SpeechResynthesis
- mapping network (isotropic -> non-isotropic), control module (yellow box), shared embedding layer for discriminator, semantic transformation matrices
- vs Style-GAN/BigGAN: Gaussian constrained encoder, stabilizes training, encodes external speakers

[Contributions]
- general framework, Gaussian -> speech
- unsupervised editing: gender characteristics, pitch, tone, emotions
- implicit sampling with speaker embeddings for GANs, divergence term, speaker encoder in generative model, external speakers

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Deep generative models have changed many fields, with several breakthroughs such as the Generative Pretrained Transformer (GPT), the Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), the Variational Autoencoder (VAE), and more recently Denoising Diffusion Models (DDPM). These models can generate realistic images, take part in conversations with humans and write intricate programs. When they are used for speech synthesis, they can produce speech that is virtually indistinguishable from human speech. But this success is mostly limited to copying the voices of the training or reference speakers. Unlike image synthesis, where models can produce realistic scenes and faces that were never seen, most speech synthesis models cannot generate new voices that were never heard. We argue that this limitation mostly comes from how the speaker encoders and neural vocoders are designed. Usually they work as deterministic modules that map speaker embeddings to the target waveforms.

Apart from the obvious advantage of being able to generate new objects, generative models also allow control over the generation process and allow manipulating the latent space to edit specific aspects of the generated objects without needing attribute labels. This is especially important for speech, because nuanced characteristics like emotion, intonation and speaker styles are hard to label. Having a speaker latent space could make more sophisticated voice editing and customization possible, which would expand the possible applications of speech synthesis a lot. But learning the speaker distribution is not easy. The reason is the intrinsic complexity of speech signals, where the characteristics specific to the speaker are entangled with the semantic content information. So we cannot just fit a distribution over speech directly and expect the model to generate new speakers while still keeping control over the content information. Disentangling content from speaker features is a necessary first step. In prior work, the authors proposed TacoSpawn, a method that fits a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) over Tacotron2 speaker embeddings to learn a prior distribution over speakers. TacoSpawn does offer the capability to generate novel speakers, but it has its own limitations. First, the speaker embedding table and the speaker generation model are parameterized separately, which keeps the synthesis modules from fully benefiting from the generative approach. Second, unlike modern deep generative models, the mixture model in TacoSpawn is trained to maximize the likelihood of the speaker embeddings and not the data likelihood, which limits the representational capability of the generative model.

In this paper we introduce VoxGenesis, which is an unsupervised generative model that learns a distribution over the voice manifold. The core of VoxGenesis is that it learns to transform a Gaussian distribution into a speech distribution, conditioned on semantic tokens. This is different from conventional GAN vocoders like Mel-GAN, HIFI-GAN and more recently SpeechResynthesis, which learn a deterministic mapping between speech features and waveforms. Figure 1 shows the differences in architecture between VoxGenesis and SpeechResynthesis. VoxGenesis has a mapping network that converts the isotropic Gaussian distribution into a non-isotropic one, so that the control module (the yellow box) can identify major variances. It also has a shared embedding layer for the discriminator and uses semantic transformation matrices, which make semantic-specific transformations of speaker attributes possible. Also, VoxGenesis is different from image generation GANs like Style-GAN or BigGAN because it integrates a Gaussian constrained encoder into the framework. This not only stabilizes training but also makes it possible to encode external speaker representations.

To summarize, our contributions are:

- • We introduce a general framework for unsupervised voice generation by transforming Gaussian distribution to speech distribution.

- • We show the potential for unsupervised editing of nuanced speaker attributes such as gender characteristics, pitch, tone and emotions.

- • We identify the implicit sampling process that comes with using speaker embeddings for GANs and propose a divergence term to constrain the distributions of the speaker embeddings. This lets the conventional speaker encoder be used as a component of a generative model, so external speakers can be encoded and then modified.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Deep generative models have revolutionized multiple fields, with several breakthroughs including the Generative Pretrained Transformer (GPT) [1], Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) [2], Variational Autoencoder (VAE) [3], and, more recently, Denoising Diffusion Models (DDPM) [4,5]. These models can generate realistic images, participate in conversations with humans and compose intricate programs. When applied to speech synthesis, they are capable of producing speech that is virtually indistinguishable from human speech [6,7,8,9,10]. However, this success is mostly confined to replicating the voices of training or reference speakers. In contrast to image synthesis, where models can produce realistic, unseen scenes and faces, most speech synthesis models are unable to generate new, unheard voices. We argue that this limitation predominantly stems from the design of speaker encoders and neural vocoders, which typically function as deterministic modules [11,12,8,13], mapping speaker embeddings to the target waveforms.

Besides the obvious advantage of being able to generate new objects, generative models also permit control over the generation process and allow latent space manipulation to edit specific aspects of the generated objects without the need for attribute labels [14,15]. This advantage is especially important in speech, where nuanced characteristics such as emotion, intonation and speaker styles are hard to label. A speaker latent space could enable more sophisticated voice editing and customization, substantially expanding the potential applications of speech synthesis. However, learning the speaker distribution is not straightforward, due to the intrinsic complexity of speech signals, in which speaker-specific characteristics are entangled with semantic content information. As such, we cannot directly fit a distribution over speech and expect the model to generate new speakers while maintaining control over the content. Disentangling content from speaker features is a necessary first step [16,17,13,18]. In [19], the authors proposed TacoSpawn, a method that fits a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) over Tacotron2 speaker embeddings to learn a prior distribution over speakers. While TacoSpawn [19] does offer the capability to generate novel speakers, it has its own set of limitations. First, the speaker embedding table and the speaker generation model are parameterized separately, which prevents the synthesis modules from fully benefiting from the generative approach. Second, unlike modern deep generative models, the mixture model in TacoSpawn is trained to maximize the likelihood of the speaker embeddings rather than the data likelihood, which limits the representational capability of the generative model.

In this paper, we introduce VoxGenesis, an unsupervised generative model that learns a distribution over the voice manifold. At its core, VoxGenesis learns to transform a Gaussian distribution into a speech distribution conditioned on semantic tokens. This contrasts with conventional GAN vocoders such as Mel-GAN [20], HIFI-GAN [21], and more recently SpeechResynthesis [11], which learn a deterministic mapping between speech features and waveforms. Figure 1 illustrates the architectural differences between VoxGenesis and SpeechResynthesis. VoxGenesis introduces a mapping network that converts the isotropic Gaussian distribution into a non-isotropic one, enabling the control module (the yellow box) to identify major variances. It also features a shared embedding layer for the discriminator and employs semantic transformation matrices, which facilitate semantic-specific transformations of speaker attributes. Furthermore, VoxGenesis differs from image generation GANs like Style-GAN or BigGAN by integrating a Gaussian constrained encoder into the framework, which not only stabilizes training but also enables the encoding of external speaker representations.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

- • We introduce a general framework for unsupervised voice generation by transforming Gaussian distribution to speech distribution.

- • We demonstrate the potential for unsupervised editing of nuanced speaker attributes such as gender characteristics, pitch, tone and emotions.

- • We identify the implicit sampling process associated with using speaker embeddings for GANs and propose a divergence term to constrain the speaker embedding distributions. This allows the conventional speaker encoder to be incorporated as a component of a generative model, facilitating the encoding and subsequent modification of external speakers.
